units.text: In-medium nucleon-nucleon cross sections from relativistic ab initio calculations
I. INTRODUCTION

Since Yukawa's pioneering proposal of the meson-exchange theory in 1935 [1], the study of strong interactions has undergone more than nine decades of extensive development.Despite numerous groundbreaking achievements in both theoretical understanding and experimental investigations, the structural and dynamical properties of strongly interacting systems, particularly those under extreme conditions of density, temperature, and isospin asymmetry, remain at the forefront of contemporary research.These fundamental questions continue to attract significant attention across multiple disciplines, including particle physics, nuclear physics, and astrophysics.

The in-medium nucleon-nucleon (NN) scattering cross sections represent fundamental physical quantities in the study on medium effects of the strong interaction.First, as the lightest strongly interacting fermions, nucleons and their bound states constitute the predominant form of visible matter in our universe.Second, NN interactions are crucial in the low-energy regime of the strong interaction, directly connected to the non-perturbative aspects of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) [2].Finally, the in-medium NN scattering cross sections govern the mean free path of nucleons [3], thereby determining the transparency and other essential transport properties of nuclear matter.

In the realm of neutron star physics, the in-medium NN scattering cross sections play a pivotal role in determining fundamental astrophysical properties through their influence on effective NN interactions, including the equation of state, mass-radius relation, and tidal deformabilities [4].In addition to these static characteristics, the in-medium NN scattering cross sections significantly impact the dynamical evolution of neutron stars by modulating key thermal properties, such as thermal conductivity, shear viscosity, and neutrino emissivity [5].Furthermore, extending the scope to include strange baryons, the in-medium baryon-baryon scattering cross sections involving hyperons are intimately related to the longstanding problem "hyperon puzzle" [6][7][8], which remains one of the most challenging issues in contemporary nuclear astrophysics.

In the context of intermediate-energy heavy-ion collisions (HICs), the in-medium NN scattering cross sections serve as crucial fundamental parameters for theoretical frameworks and transport model simulations [9][10][11].At the microscopic level, these cross sections govern both the collision rates and angular dependence in NN collisions, thereby influencing the production mechanisms, dynamical evolution, and spatial distribution of emitted particles, as well as the emergence and characteristics of collective flow.Experimentally, the measured final-state particle multiplicities, isotopic compositions, and kinematic distributions exhibit significant sensitivity to the in-medium modifications of NN interactions.This dependence enables the extraction of essential nuclear matter properties through systematic comparisons between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements in HICs.

The accurate determination of in-medium NN scattering cross sections presents significant theoretical challenges [12,13], primarily stemming from their complex dependence on various parameters.These include not only the intrinsic properties of the colliding nucleon pair, such as relative momentum, center-of-mass motion, and isospin projections, but also the environmental conditions characterized by baryon density, temperature, and isospin asymmetry.Current theoretical studies typically incorporate medium modifications through either empirical density-dependent scaling factors applied to vacuum cross sections [14][15][16][17] or by employing effective nucleon masses in nuclear medium [18][19][20].While these phenomenological approaches provide valuable connections to experimental data, they fall short of capturing the fundamental nature of strongly interacting systems.A more comprehensive understanding requires ab initio calculations that simultaneously combine realistic NN interactions with advanced many-body techniques [21,22].The realistic NN interactions, which accurately reproduce free-space NN scattering data and two-as well as three-body bound state, can be systematically classified into three main categories based on their theoretical foundations.The first category comprises potential models constructed through operator analysis, exemplified by the Argonne V18 potential [23].The second category utilizes meson-exchange models, such as the Bonn potential [24] and its refined version, the CD-Bonn potential [25].The third category encompasses chiral interactions derived from chiral effective field theory, which has gained increasing attention in recent years [26,27].Comprehensive reviews and detailed discussions of these interaction models can be found in several authoritative references [22,24,28,29].

Based on realistic NN interactions, various microscopic many-body approaches have been developed to investigate in-medium NN elastic and inelastic scattering cross sections.These include the Brueckner-Hartree-Fock (BHF) theory [30,31], the Green's function approach [32,33], the variational method [18], the relativistic Boltzmann-Uehling-Uhlenbeck approach [34,35], and the relativistic Brueckner-Hartree-Fock (RBHF) theory [36][37][38][39].General agree-ment on several key features have been reached: the reduction of cross sections for low energy scattering in nuclear medium, their strong enhancement near the Fermi surface, and the isospin symmetry breaking to some extend.However, quantitative predictions vary depending on the extent of medium effects incorporated in each theoretical framework.The RBHF theory distinguishes itself by consistently accounting for multiple crucial effects: Pauli exclusion principle, energy-momentum dispersion relations, and relativistic dynamics [40][41][42].This comprehensive treatment enables RBHF theory to successfully reproduce nuclear matter saturation properties [43,44], a longstanding benchmark for nuclear many-body theories.The superior performance of RBHF theory can be attributed to its inherent inclusion of density-dependent three-body forces through virtual nucleon-antinucleon pair excitations, commonly known as the Z-diagram [45].

The RBHF theory is fundamentally characterized by its double iterative structure involving the effective interaction G matrix and single-particle potentials [46].Historically, RBHF implementations were restricted to positive-energy solutions of the Dirac equation, with negative-energy state contributions incorporated through approximate treatments.This limitation hindered the rigorous determination of single-particle potentials from the G matrix.Recent theoretical advancements have overcome this constraint by implementing fully self-consistent RBHF calculations in the full Dirac space, explicitly including both positiveand negative-energy states [47][48][49].This comprehensive approach not only provides unambiguous determination of nucleon single-particle properties but also significantly enhances the precision of G matrix calculations through iterative solutions of the in-medium NN scattering equation.These developments offer a promising framework for the theoretical investigation of in-medium NN scattering cross sections.

In this work, we aim to derive the in-medium NN scattering cross sections with the RBHF theory in the full Dirac space.This paper is organized as follows: Section II details the theoretical formalism, including the RBHF implementation in the full Dirac space and the methodology for calculating in-medium NN scattering observables.Section III presents and analyzes the numerical results, focusing on medium-modified phase shifts, angular distributions, and integrated cross sections.The concluding section, Section IV, summarizes
the key findings and discusses potential future developments in this research direction.
II. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK A. The RBHF theory in the full Dirac space

The starting point of the RBHF calculations is the realistic NN interaction.Here we use the one-boson-exchange potential (OBEP) [24], which describes the NN interactions by mediating six mesons with masses below 1 GeV.Guided by symmetry principles and simplicity, the most commonly used interaction Lagrangians that coupled these meson fields φ to nucleon fields ψ are written as follows
L NNs = g s ψψφ (s) ,(1a)
L NNpv = − f ps m ps ψγ 5 γ µ ψ∂ µ φ (ps) ,(1b)
L NNv = − g v ψγ µ ψφ (v) µ − f v 4M ψσ µν ψ ∂ µ φ (v) ν − ∂ ν φ (v) µ .(1c)
The scalar (s) mesons σ and δ are coupled to nucleon fields through the scalar coupling.

For pseudoscalar (ps) mesons η and π, the pseudovector (pv) coupling is adopted, while for vector (v) mesons ω and ρ, both the vector coupling and tensor coupling are considered.In Eq. ( 1), the isospin indexes for isovector mesons are not shown for simplicity.The g's and f 's are coupling constants, which are nicely constrained by experimental data of NN bound and scattering states.Although chiral forces are more popular in these days, we emphasize that the OBEP is the most economical and quantitative phenomenology for describing the NN interaction [28].Bonn potentials have three different parametrizations of the OBEP, which are named by Bonn A, B, and C. The main difference among the three parametrizations lies in the cutoff parameter of the πN coupling, which leads to the weakest tensor force for Bonn A and the strongest tensor force for Bonn C [50].

In the RBHF theory, the nucleon inside the nuclear medium is viewed as a dressed particle in consequence of its interaction with the surrounding nucleons.The single-particle motion of nucleons in the nuclear medium is depicted by the Dirac equation

(p) = U S (p) + γ 0 U 0 (p) + γ • pU V (p).(3)

The quantities U S (p), U 0 (p), and U V (p) are the scalar potential, timelike, and spacelike parts of the vector potential respectively with p = |p| the magnitude of nucleon momentum.p = p/|p| is the unit vector parallel to the momentum p.By virtue of the following effective quantities:

To conclude this section, we would like to emphasize three key points that are related to the relativistic scattering equation (10).First, Pauli blocking effects are incorporated via the Pauli operator.Second, the starting energy and the single-particle energies in the denominator are calculated using effective quantities, which account for dispersion effects.

Third, the NN interaction matrix elements are constructed with effective Dirac spinors in the medium, capturing the essential density dependence.By including Pauli blocking effects, dispersion effects, and relativistic medium effects, the RBHF theory provides a promising framework for investigating medium effects of strong interaction from ab initio calculations.

III. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

In this section, we present the numerical results obtained using the RBHF theory with the Bonn A potential, which accurately describes the nuclear matter properties at the saturation point.These results include medium-modified phase shifts, angular distributions, and integrated cross sections.
A. Phase shifts in nuclear medium

Figure 1 displays the in-medium neutron-proton (np) phase shifts for the 1 S 0 , 3 S 1 , and 3 D 1 channels as functions of the laboratory energy E lab up to the pion-production threshold (∼ 300 MeV).The results are presented for three distinct baryon densities: ρ = 0.5ρ 0 , ρ 0 , and 1.5ρ 0 , where the saturation density ρ 0 is 0.16 fm −3 .The total momentum and isospin asymmetry are set to P = 0 and α = 0, respectively.These specific channels are selected to examine the medium effects on potential bound states, given the presence of a virtual state in the 1 S 0 channel and a true bound state, the deuteron, in the 3 SD 1 mixed channel.As illustrated in Figure 1, the in-medium phase shifts demonstrate distinctive characteristics: The np scattering phase shifts for the 1 S 0 , 3 S 1 , and 3 D 1 channels as functions of the laboratory energy.In each panel, the green short-dashed, red solid, and blue short-dotted lines represent the results at densities ρ = 0.5ρ 0 , ρ 0 , and 1.5ρ 0 , respectively.For comparison, the phase shifts in free space are shown as black dashed lines.The total momentum and isospin asymmetry are set as P = 0 and α = 0.
they approach zero at E lab = 0, indicating the absence of bound states in these channels in nuclear matter.

A notable feature is the sharp increase followed by a decrease in the 3 S 1 phase shift at low laboratory energies, which becomes more prominent at lower densities, indicating a gradual convergence toward the free-space behavior.This density-dependence trend also highlights the difficulties encountered in RBHF calculations for densities below ρ = 0.08 fm −3 , where the emergence of nucleon bound states leads to inhomogeneities in the nuclear medium.

Furthermore, a significant enhancement of the phase shift is observed at laboratory energies near the Fermi momentum, particularly evident in the 3 S 1 channel and ρ = ρ 0 .For symmetric nuclear matter at ρ = 0.16 fm −3 , the nucleon Fermi momentum is k F = 1.33 fm −1 , corresponding to a laboratory energy of E lab ≈ 147 MeV.In the middle panel of Fig. 1, the enhancement is observed around 150 MeV.This enhancement indicates a stronger interaction between nucleons at these energies, which can be attributed to the increased overlap of their wave functions near the Fermi surface, leading to more pronounced quantum effects such as Pauli blocking and medium modifications.

To investigate whether the observed enhancement is specific to certain channels, Fig. 2 presents the pp phase shifts for the 3 P 0,1,2 channels, which do not exhibit virtual or bound states in free space.It is important to note that only the phase shifts arising from the strong interaction are considered, with the Coulomb interaction explicitly excluded.As shown in Fig. 2, the enhancements remain evident, suggesting that this phenomenon is a general feature rather than being limited to specific channels.The red solid, blue short-dashed, pink short-dotted, and green short-dash-dotted lines correspond to the total momenta P = 0, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 fm −1 , respectively.The phase shifts in free space are also given as black dashed lines for comparison.The density is fixed at ρ = ρ 0 .

In Fig. 3, the in-medium np phase shifts for the 3 S 1 channel are shown for various total momenta, P = 0, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 fm −1 .It is evident that the enhancement in the phase shift diminishes rapidly for finite total momenta, as demonstrated by the blue short-dashed curve corresponding to P = 1.0 fm −1 .This suggests that the peak is closely associated with the Pauli operator Q av (k, P ), where P plays a critical role.At P = 0, the Pauli operator acts as a step function with values of either 0 or 1, leading to a sudden change in the integral for k in Eq. ( 10) at k = k F .In contrast, for finite P , the Pauli operator is smoothed, resulting in a more gradual variation in the integral in Eq. ( 10).This provides a technical explanation of the observed enhancement in phase shifts.

Taking a comprehensive view of the figures discussed above, if one disregards the enhancement near the Fermi surface for P = 0, a general suppression of phase shifts in the medium relative to their free-space values can be observed.For 1 S 0 and 3 S 1 channels in Fig. 1 and the 3 P 0 channel in Fig. 2, this suppression leads to an earlier transition from attractive to repulsive interactions, as indicated by the shift from positive to negative values.For the 3 P 2 and

3 D 1 channels, the medium effects tend to reduce the magnitudes of the phase shifts, while for the 3 P 1 channel, the in-medium phase shift exhibit larger absolute values.Although the medium effects vary across partial waves, they become more pronounced at higher densities, as illustrated in Figs. 1 and 2. On the other hand, the phase shifts show limited sensitivity to the total momenta P , particularly at higher laboratory energies, as seen in Fig. 3.This suggests that the influence of P on the in-medium NN interaction becomes less significant at higher energies.

The preceding analysis has focused on symmetric nuclear matter.In Fig. 4, we present the np, pp, and nn scattering phase shifts for the 1 S 0 channel as functions of the laboratory energy, with isospin asymmetries α = 0, 0.4, and 0.8.Notably, the phase shifts exhibit minimal dependence on isospin asymmetry.For the nn pair, the phase shifts can be regarded as isospin independent.A slight variation in phase shifts with α is observed for the pp pair at E lab ∼ 50 MeV.In the case of np pair, the results align more closely with the nn data than with the pp results, highlighting the predominant role of neutrons in asymmetric nuclear systems, as expected.MeV, and three baryon densities, ρ = 0.5ρ 0 , ρ 0 , and 1.5ρ 0 .The total momentum and isospin asymmetry are fixed at P = 1.0 fm −1 and α = 0.In comparison to the free-space results as shown with black dashed lines, the in-medium np differential cross sections are suppressed in most cases.They also display a pronounced parabolic profile dominated by enhanced backward-angle scattering.This backward-angle amplification, which becomes more evident with higher densities, arises from spin-isospin exchange interactions inherent to the np system.As E lab increases, both the magnitudes of dσ np /dΩ and its in-medium suppression gradually diminish.Notably, at E lab = 300 MeV, the differential scattering cross sections for 1.5ρ 0 in the range of 30 • ≤ θ cm ≤ 60 • exceed their free-space counterparts, marking a reversal of the suppression trend observed at lower energies.

[63].fermion pairs scattering with respect to θ cm = 90 • , only results for θ cm ≤ 90 • are represented.

In contrast to the parabolic angular dependence observed in np scattering (Fig. 5), the pp cross sections displays a relatively uniform angular distribution.In free space as shown with black dashed lines, dσ/dΩ generally decreases as E lab rises from 50 to 300 MeV, though the rate of decline diminishes with increasing energy.In the nuclear medium, the interplay between energy and densities dependencies introduce greater complexity.At E lab = 50 and 100 MeV, dσ/dΩ initially decreases for subsaturation densities (ρ ≤ ρ 0 ) but rises at ρ = 1.5ρ 0 .For E lab = 200 and 300 MeV, dσ/dΩ exhibits a continuous rise across the density range 0.5ρ 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 1.5ρ 0 , ultimately exceeding the corresponding values in free space.Similar tendency for the medium enhancement of pp differential cross sections has been obtained at E lab = 250 MeV in Fig. 3 of Ref. [37].A notable characteristic observed in all systems is the sharp decline of σ np with increasing E lab below 200 MeV, followed by a plateau around 25 mb at higher energies (200 ≤ E lab ≤ 300 MeV).This rapid decrease at low E lab aligns with findings from Ref. [13] using BHF calculations.However, unlike the plateau observed here, the BHF results exhibit a gradual increase at high E lab .

Consistent with the phase-shift analysis in Subsection III A, significant enhancements in σ np are observed near the Fermi surface.In the left panel, which depicts np scattering in symmetric nuclear matter, the most significant enhancement occurs at ρ = 0.16 fm −3 , in qualitative agreement with earlier nonrelativistic BHF calculations [30].These enhancements are primarily relevant for total momentum close to zero.Consequently, they are absent in the latest BHF calculations on in-medium scattering cross sections in Ref. [13],
where the total momenta of the colliding pairs are constrained to values no less than 0.9 fm −1 .
Excluding these special enhancements, medium effects generally lead to a reduction in σ np compared to the values in free space.

Figure 7 further reveals that the density dependence of σ np is entangled with the total momentum dependence.For scattering in the center-of-mass frame (P = 0), the total cross sections at different densities largely coincide, except for the aforementioned enhancements.

At higher total momenta (P = 1.0 fm −1 ), deviations between cross sections at varying densities become noticeable, particularly at low laboratory energies.These differences grow more pronounced as the total momentum increases to P = 2.0 fm −1 .Extending to asymmetric nuclear matter, Fig. 8 displays the total in-medium np cross sections at baryon densities ρ = 0.5 and 1.5ρ 0 for isospin asymmetries α = 0, 0.4, and 0.8.

The results reveal a remarkably weak dependence on isospin asymmetry.Across the transition from sub-saturation to supra-saturation densities, the cross sections in symmetric and asymmetric nuclear matter exhibit close agreement.This suggests that the parametrizations of np cross sections can be largely simplified by neglecting the α-dependence.To examine if the weak isospin dependence observed in np scattering also applies to identical fermions scattering, Fig. 9 presents the total pp cross sections.Overall, the isospin independence remains evident.Interestingly, in contrast to the medium suppression of np scattering persisting up to E lab = 300 MeV, the pp total scattering cross sections exceed their free-space values at E lab ∼ 150 MeV for 1.5ρ 0 .

To further explore the differences in pp, np, and nn cross sections in asymmetric nuclear matter, in Figs. 10 and 11, we present the ratios of total in-medium cross sections, σ pp /σ np and σ pp /σ nn , respectively.For the former, the free-space ratio already deviates from unity, which can be attributed to the fact that np scattering involves contributions from both isospin T = 0 and T = 1 channels, whereas pp (and nn) scattering is restricted to T = 1 interactions.The ratio σ pp /σ np is mostly influenced by variations in laboratory energy.As E lab increase, the ratio approaches unity and exceeds it at E lab = 150 MeV for suprasaturation densities.From 50 MeV to 300 MeV, this ratio remains relatively insensitive to changes in isospin asymmetry.This can be utilized in the future parametrizations.

As illustrated in Fig. 11, the pp and nn cross sections exhibit approximate isospin symmetry, particularly for α ≤ 0.4.For α = 0.8, the ratio σ pp /σ nn fluctuates around its value in symmetric nuclear matter.Overall, for the saturation density and below, as well as supra-saturation densities with large laboratory energy E lab ≥ 150 MeV, the magnitudes of pp scattering cross sections tend to exceed those of nn scattering.For supra-saturation densities with 50 MeV ≤ E lab ≤ 150 MeV, nn cross sections have larger values.The observed nontrivial variations in the ratios of pp, np, and nn cross sections demonstrate that the conventional approach, which assumes identical matrix elements for NN interactions in free space and nuclear medium and derives in-medium cross sections through simple scaling of effective masses [19,20], fails to provide an adequate description of nuclear many-body dynamics.
IV. SUMMARY AND PROSPECTIVE

In summary, this study provides a microscopic investigation of in-medium nucleonnucleon (NN) scattering cross sections using the relativistic Brueckner-Hartree-Fock (RBHF) theory with the Bonn potential.By solving the RBHF equations in the full Dirac space, namely incorporating both positive-and negative-energy solutions of the Dirac equation, we derive the complex G matrix in nuclear matter and subsequently calculate the S matrix elements, scattering amplitudes, and observables including phase shifts, differential cross sections, and total cross sections for pp, nn, and np systems.Our results demonstrate fundamental modifications to NN interactions in dense hadronic environments.The absence of bound states in nuclear matter is revealed through characteristic phase-shift patterns in both 1 S 0 and 3 S 1 channels, while medium suppression effects exhibit stronger sensitivity to baryon density than to isospin asymmetry.Distinct angular dependencies emerge between pp and np scattering, with the former displaying quasi-isotropic distributions and the latter showing pronounced backward-angle enhancement due to spin-isospin exchange interactions.

Notably, resonant-like amplifications of total cross sections and phase shifts are observed near the Fermi momentum and zero total momentum, correlating with the emergence of imaginary components in the G-matrix induced by multi scattering in nuclear medium.

The analysis underscores the complicated multi-parameter dependence of in-medium cross sections on laboratory energy E lab , total momentum P , density ρ, and isospin asymmetry α.To improve the practical applicability of our results, we are developing a systematic parametrization scheme of σ(E lab , P, ρ, α) to facilitate implementation in transport models.This parametrization is also helpful with the mean field calculated self-consistently starting from the same realistic NN interactions [48].Future efforts will extend this framework to include Deltas in the scattering processes [64][65][66], providing critical elastic and inelastic cross sections essential for modeling intermediate-energy heavy ion collision simulations.

Additionally, recent years have witnessed important progress in developing relativistic chiral nuclear forces [67].Microscopic in-medium cross sections starting from that would be more promising considering its closer relation to the chiral symmetry and its breaking in lowenergy quantum chromodynamics.
